observed.text:
L-lyxose is an uncommon sugar in nature, and wild-type Escherichia coli can not utilize it as a sole source of carbon and energy. However, mutations can arise that allow Escherichia coli to metabolize L-lyxose through the use of enzymes of the rhamnose, arabinose and 2,3-diketo-L-gulonate systems.

L-lyxose enters the cell through the rhaT-encoded rhamnose transporter. It is then isomerized to L-xylulose by L-rhamnose isomerase.

Two types of mutations then allow further utilization of L-xylulose. Not shown here, a mutated from of rhamnulokinase can phosphorylate L-xylulose, yielding L-xylulose-1-phosphate. Further metabolism to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glycolate occurs through the rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase and aldehyde dehydrogenase A, NAD-linked enzymes. These products can enter glycolate degradation and glycolysis [Badia91].

As shown here, L-xylulose can be phosphorylated by L-xylulose kinase in a mutant in which YiaJ, the repressor for the yiaKLMNO-lyxK-sgbHUE operon, has been disrupted [Sanchez94]. L-xylulose-5-phosphate is then further metabolized by putative L-xylulose 5-phosphate 3-epimerase (so far only a predicted function) and either of two L-ribulose 5-phosphate 4-epimerases (SgbE or AraD) to D-xylulose-5-phosphate, which then enters the pentose phosphate pathway (non-oxidative branch) I [Badia98, Ibanez00].

The enzymes of L-rhamnose degradation I and L-arabinose degradation I are inducible by L-lyxose as well [Badia91, Ibanez00].

Review: Mayer, C. and W. Boos, Hexose/Pentose and Hexitol/Pentitol Metabolism, EcoSal Module 3.4.1 [EcoSal]

assertion: The 2000 study genetically implicated yiaR but failed to detect 3-epimerase activity, including a purified GST-based preparation. It retained the assignment as tentative, with possible instability or missing cofactor.

observed.xml: In the metabolic system under study here, a 3-epimerase activity could convert the l-xylulose-5-phosphate generated by l-xylulose kinase into the l-ribulose-5-phosphate substrate of YiaS (Fig. 2). However, all attempts to obtain experimental evidence of the 3-epimerase activity have been unsuccessful so far. This included the purification of YiaR through its fusion to the protein glutathione S-transferase and separation of the fused protein by affinity chromatography with glutathione to assay the enzymatic activity. The studies performed on YiaR did not rule out its possible role as a 3-epimerase and suggested either a low stability of YiaR or the lack of a key cofactor required for activity and/or stability.

assertion: Complementation of the JA198 araD yiaS double mutant by plasmids carrying either gene restored the examined metabolism, supporting alternative 4-epimerase functions.

observed.xml: The induction of the ara system by l-lyxose and the high similarity displayed by YiaS and AraD suggest that AraD could complement the YiaS function in strain JA196. To determine whether AraD complemented YiaS function, the araD mutation of strain MC4100 was transferred into the genetic background of strain JA196 (yiaS::cat) by the following strategy. (i) A Tn10 marker was transduced from strain CAG12095 (13) into strain MC4100, and tetracycline-resistant transductants that retained the inability to utilize l-arabinose were selected. (ii) One of these transductants (strain JA197) was subsequently used to transduce the two linked markers into strain JA196. A double mutant (strain JA198) was isolated and transformed with plasmids containing yiaS or araD and tested for its ability to utilize both l-lyxose and l-arabinose. None of the transformants analyzed displayed impairment in either of these metabolisms, showing that the 4-epimerase function could be supplied by either of the two YiaS and AraD proteins.

assertion: Enzyme genes were PCR-amplified from MG1655 genomic DNA and cloned into modified pET15b encoding an N-terminal 10His tag.

observed.xml: The genes encoding SgaE and SgbE, as well as those encoding SgaH, SgbH, SgaU, SgbU, YiaK, and LyxK, also discussed in this paper, were PCR amplified from genomic DNA isolated from E. coli strain MG1655 using Platinum Pfx DNA polymerase (Life Technologies). A typical PCR mixture (100 μl) contained 1 ng of genomic DNA, 10 μl of 10× Pfx amplification buffer (Life Technologies), 1 mM MgSO4, 0.4 mM concentrations of each of the four deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs), 40 pmol of each primer (Table 1), and 5 U of Platinum Pfx DNA polymerase. The genes were amplified using a PTC-200 gradient thermal cycler (MJ Research), with the following parameters: 94°C for 2 min; followed by 40 cycles of 94°C for 1 min, a gradient annealing temperature range of 45 to 60°C for 1 min 15 s and 68°C for 2 min; and a final extension of 68°C for 10 min. The amplified genes were cloned into a modified pET15-b (Novagen) vector in which the N-terminal His tag contains 10 instead of the usual 6 His residues.

assertion: Purified SgbE catalyzed the L-ribulose 5-phosphate to D-xylulose 5-phosphate reaction in a coupled assay; The purified preparation independently extends the earlier cell-extract evidence.

observed.xml: Both SgaE and SgbE catalyzed the epimerization of l-ribulose 5-phosphate to d-xylulose 5-phosphate, using the established coupled enzyme assay for AraD (transketolase, triose phosphate isomerase, and α-glycerolphosphate dehydrogenase [9–11;]). The kinetic constants for the SgaE- and SgbE-catalyzed reactions, presented in Table 2, are comparable to those reported for AraD (9–11) (values not shown), so we conclude that SgaE and SgbE are l-ribulose 5-phosphate 4-epimerases. <comment datatype="string">L-ribulose 5-phosphate 4-epimerase catalyzes the third step in the pathway for degradation of L-arabinose, the epimerization at the C4 carbon to form D-xylulose-5-phosphate, which enters the <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=NONOXIPENT-PWY">pentose phosphate pathway (non-oxidative branch) I</a>.
<p>
The enzyme catalyzes epimerization via a carbon-carbon bond cleavage analogous to a class II aldolase reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9548961">Johnson98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769138">Lee00</a>].  The H97N and other mutants can catalyze an aldolase reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9548961">Johnson98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769139">Lee00a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732896">Samuel01</a>].  The binding site for Zn<sup>2+</sup>, the physiological metal cofactor, has been identified by sequence similarity and mutagenesis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769139">Lee00a</a>] as well as in the crystal structure [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>].  Mutagenesis of the predicted phosphate-binding pocket results in a significant increase in K<sub>m</sub>, and Asp120 was identified as one of two key catalytic acid/base residues [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732896">Samuel01</a>].
<p>
The enzyme was crystallized [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8520491">Andersson95</a>], and crystal structures of the wild type [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>] and a mutant enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732896">Samuel01</a>] have been solved.  Consistent with its aldolase-type reaction mechanism, the structure shows close overall similarity to that of L-fuculose-1-phosphate aldolase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>].
<p>
(Note: Several of the recent studies, including crystallization of the enzyme, appear to be using the enzyme from <i>E. coli</i> B/r UP1000 (gene originally cloned by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3549454">Lee86</a>]) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769138">Lee00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769139">Lee00a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732896">Samuel01</a>].)  Most studies of the enzyme and its genetics were done in <i>E. coli</i> B/r.  
<p>
Earlier studies of the enzyme from <i>E. coli</i> B/r described its purification [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4879898">Lee68</a>], its catalytic mechanism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4560420">Davis72</a>] and summarized its properties [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/236468">Gielow75</a>]. The nucleotide sequence of the coding region of <i>araD</i> from <i>E. coli</i> K-12 W3110 was shown to be 97% identical to that of <i>E. coli</i> B/r, and the deduced amino acid sequences showed 98.7% identity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2251150">Mineno90</a>].
<p>
AraD from <i>E. coli</i> DH1 (a K-12 derivative) forms a stable homotetramer as determined by size exclusion chromatography [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9548961">Johnson98</a>].
<p>
Metabolic engineering work in yeast has utilized <i>E. coli</i> <i>araD</i> and <i>araB</i>, and <i>Bacillus subtilis</i> or <i>B. licheniformis araA</i> in the fermentation of L-arabinose to ethanol [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12839792">Becker03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18263741">Wiedemann08</a>].
<p>
Transcription of the <i>araBAD</i> operon is induced in the presence of L-arabinose by the transcription factor AraC [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1093171">Casadaban75</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7768852">Johnson95</a>].  <i>araBAD</i> expression can also induced by L-lyxose [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10913097">Ibanez00</a>].
<p>
<i>araD</i> mutants can not utilize L-arabinose for growth [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13829634">Gross59</a>] and accumulate L-ribulose 5-phosphate when incubated with L-arabinose [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13890280">Englesberg62</a>].</comment>

L-ribulose 5-phosphate 4-epimerase catalyzes the third step in the pathway for degradation of L-arabinose, the epimerization at the C4 carbon to form D-xylulose-5-phosphate, which enters the pentose phosphate pathway (non-oxidative branch) I.

The enzyme catalyzes epimerization via a carbon-carbon bond cleavage analogous to a class II aldolase reaction [Johnson98, Lee00]. The H97N and other mutants can catalyze an aldolase reaction [Johnson98, Lee00a, Samuel01]. The binding site for Zn2+, the physiological metal cofactor, has been identified by sequence similarity and mutagenesis [Lee00a] as well as in the crystal structure [Luo01]. Mutagenesis of the predicted phosphate-binding pocket results in a significant increase in Km, and Asp120 was identified as one of two key catalytic acid/base residues [Samuel01].

The enzyme was crystallized [Andersson95], and crystal structures of the wild type [Luo01] and a mutant enzyme [Samuel01] have been solved. Consistent with its aldolase-type reaction mechanism, the structure shows close overall similarity to that of L-fuculose-1-phosphate aldolase [Luo01].

(Note: Several of the recent studies, including crystallization of the enzyme, appear to be using the enzyme from E. coli B/r UP1000 (gene originally cloned by [Lee86]) [Lee00, Lee00a, Luo01, Samuel01].) Most studies of the enzyme and its genetics were done in E. coli B/r.

Earlier studies of the enzyme from E. coli B/r described its purification [Lee68], its catalytic mechanism [Davis72] and summarized its properties [Gielow75]. The nucleotide sequence of the coding region of araD from E. coli K-12 W3110 was shown to be 97% identical to that of E. coli B/r, and the deduced amino acid sequences showed 98.7% identity [Mineno90].

AraD from E. coli DH1 (a K-12 derivative) forms a stable homotetramer as determined by size exclusion chromatography [Johnson98].

Metabolic engineering work in yeast has utilized E. coli araD and araB, and Bacillus subtilis or B. licheniformis araA in the fermentation of L-arabinose to ethanol [Becker03, Wiedemann08].

Transcription of the araBAD operon is induced in the presence of L-arabinose by the transcription factor AraC [Casadaban75, Johnson95]. araBAD expression can also induced by L-lyxose [Ibanez00].

araD mutants can not utilize L-arabinose for growth [Gross59] and accumulate L-ribulose 5-phosphate when incubated with L-arabinose [Englesberg62].

observed.xml: Transcription of the yiaK-S genes as a single unit was also supported by the properties of lacZ fusions presented in Fig. 1. assertion: The study supports CRP-cAMP activation of yiaK-S through site 1 centered at -106. Binding at site 2 had unknown function and supplies no signed regulatory edge.

observed.xml: Our results indicate that the yiaK-S operon is regulated by carbon sources. As shown, succinate increases and glucose reduces its expression in the absence of the repressor. This promoter strongly responds to glucose catabolite repression through the Crp site 1; in contrast, the yiaJ promoter, which overlaps with the yiaK-S promoter and is transcribed divergently from it, responds to the same conditions with increased expression. The mechanism for this yiaJ activation seems to be based on the nonoccupancy of Crp site 1 by the Crp-cAMP complex, hence releasing the obstruction to yiaJ transcription. In this way, catabolite repression of yiaK-S expression is coordinately helped by the increase in the repressor synthesis. In the absence of glucose, Crp-cAMP complex binds to Crp site 1 activating yiaK-S expression and obstructing the yiaJ-encoded repressor expression and synthesis. In spite of the binding observed to Crp site 2, its function remains unknown.

assertion: The study supports CRP-cAMP activation of yiaK-S through site 1 centered at -106. Binding at site 2 had unknown function and supplies no signed regulatory edge.

observed.xml: Our results indicate that the yiaK-S operon is regulated by carbon sources. As shown, succinate increases and glucose reduces its expression in the absence of the repressor. This promoter strongly responds to glucose catabolite repression through the Crp site 1; in contrast, the yiaJ promoter, which overlaps with the yiaK-S promoter and is transcribed divergently from it, responds to the same conditions with increased expression. The mechanism for this yiaJ activation seems to be based on the nonoccupancy of Crp site 1 by the Crp-cAMP complex, hence releasing the obstruction to yiaJ transcription. In this way, catabolite repression of yiaK-S expression is coordinately helped by the increase in the repressor synthesis. In the absence of glucose, Crp-cAMP complex binds to Crp site 1 activating yiaK-S expression and obstructing the yiaJ-encoded repressor expression and synthesis. In spite of the binding observed to Crp site 2, its function remains unknown.

The himA::cat and the himD3::cat alleles were transferred from strain HN1491 and strain K2704 to a JA134 background by P1 transduction, yielding strains JA184 and JA185. Introduction of each of these IHF mutations produced a fourfold decrease in β-galactosidase activity in these mutant strains compared with that of the isogenic wild type (data not shown). These results suggest that IHF activates yiaK-S expression.

<comment datatype="string">The basal level of <i>rsd</i> transcription is maintained by using the downstream rsdp2 promoter recognized by E&sigma;<sup>70</sup>. On the basis of sequence similarity and unique expression patterns, such as the inverse relationship with the growth rate, the rsdp2 promoter can be classified as a member of the gearbox family of promoters, but it cannot be transcribed by E&sigma;<sup>38</sup> <i>in vivo</i> or <i>in vitro</i>. Under certain circumstances, the upstream sequence including the rsdp1 promoter exerts an inhibitory effect on the rsdp2 function, because the deletion of the rsdp1 region results in an increase in transcription from the downstream rsdp2 promoter. The mechanism of inhibition by the upstream sequence remains unsolved.</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Based on ChIP-microarray analysis, it was shown that StpA binds to the promoter region in <i>appY</i>p2 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8655536">Atlung96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19151137">Uyar09</a>]. qRT-PCR revealed a strong 75-fold repression of <i>appY</i> by H-NS and more than 1,000-fold repression by H-NS/StpA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29424946">Rangarajan18</a>].
<p>
Transcription directed across H-NS binding regions relieves H-NS-mediated (and H-NS/StpA-mediated) repression of promoters such as <i>proV</i>p3, <i>pdeL</i>p3, and <i>appY</i>p2, and there is a correlation between transcription across the H-NS-bound region and derepression where RNA polymerase is able to remodel the H-NS complex and/or dislodge H-NS from the DNA and thus relieve repression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29424946">Rangarajan18</a>].
</comment>

<comment datatype="string">~90% of the <i>ptsG</i> mRNA is transcribed from a major promoter, P1 (ptsGp1) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9767573">Plumbridge98a</a>].
<p>
A third promoter in the region located between <i>ptsG</i>p1 and <i>ptsG</i>p2 was identified by <i>in vitro</i> transcription and by RNA polymerase footprinting techniques, as well as <i>in vivo</i> by S1 analysis and fusions with a <i>lacZ</i> reporter gene [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20668389">Pennetier10</a>]. It expresses a transcript antisense to <i>ptsG</i> that has characteristics more like a divergently expressed cryptic unstable transcript (CUT) than a prokaryotic sRNA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20668389">Pennetier10</a>].
<p>
<i>ptsG</i>p1 was validated experimentally in aerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146601">Chung13</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">ArcA is a dual transcriptional regulator for <b>A</b>noxic <b>r</b>edox <b>c</b>ontrol [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2964639">Iuchi88</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8412675">Iuchi93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7855430">Gunsalus94</a>]. It acts primarily as a negative transcriptional regulator under anaerobic conditions. ArcA represses operons involved in respiratory metabolism, including those that encode products such as the tricarboxylic acid cycle enzymes, enzymes of the glyoxylate shunt, and enzymes of the pathway for fatty acid degradation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2070418">Iuchi91</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7855430">Gunsalus94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1812811">Lin91</a>]. In addition, ArcA acts as a repressor for <i>rpoS</i> transcription [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16291649">Mika05</a>]. ArcA also activates a few operons encoding proteins involved in fermentative metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8071220">Brondsted94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8892825">Lynch96</a>]. It has been identified as global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. Microarray analyses have identified a large number of genes affected by ArcA and have revealed that the Arc system and the FNR regulatory network overlap to a much greater extent than previously estimated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15699038">Salmon05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14711822">Liu04a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15838044">Perrenoud05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. It has been suggested that the most significant role of ArcA is under microaerobic conditions, while that of FNR is under more strictly anaerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12486057">Alexeeva03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15669087">Levanon05</a>]. For full expression of <i>arcA</i> both FNR and ArcA are required [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8022271">Compan94</a>]. Distinct functional roles for both regulators have been proposed, and it has been shown that there is little direct coregulation of the two [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>].
<p>
ArcA is a response regulator and is activated as a DNA-binding protein by phosphorylation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11527965">Jeon01</a>]. The cognate sensor kinase ArcB is membrane associated and has three cytoplasmic domains; a transmitter, a receiver, and a phosphotransfer (HPt) domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7957084">Ishige94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1597416">Iuchi92a</a>]. Under anaerobic conditions ArcA is phosphorylated in a phosphorelay reaction that involves phosphotransfer from the autophosphorylated transmitter domain of ArcB to the receiver and Hpt domain of ArcB and finally to the receiver domain of ArcA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10851007">Kwon00c</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8825099">Tsuzuki95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9286997">Georgellis97</a>]. Autophosphorylation of ArcB is stimulated by effectors such as d-lactate, pyruvate, and acetate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10585483">Georgellis99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10585483">Georgellis99</a>]. Under aerobic conditions, the autokinase activity of ArcB is inhibited by quinone electron carriers [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423658">Georgellis01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15326287">Malpica04</a>], and unphosphorylated ArcB promotes the dephosphorylation of ArcA-P by a reverse phosphorelay reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9830034">Georgellis98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15838055">PenaSandoval05</a>]. It has been suggested that ArcA may also be subject to cross-regulation by other, unknown sensor kinases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16291649">Mika05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12366850">Oshima02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17213678">Kato07a</a>]. Z nucleotides [ZMP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-monophosphate) and/or ZTP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-triphosphate)] can act as direct phosphodonors to ArcA <i>in vivo</i>, activating it in an ArcB-independent manner [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33318202">VazquezCiros20</a>].
<p>
ArcA is a member of the OmpR/PhoB subfamily of response regulators and consists of an N-terminal receiver domain and a C-terminal helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9205844">Mizuno97</a>]. The crystal structures of the receiver domain of ArcA in the presence and absence of the phosphoryl analog BeF<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> have been solved [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15876365">ToroRoman05a</a>]. In the crystal structures, the receiver domain forms a symmetric dimer.
<p>
ArcA appears to be S-nitrosylated on Cys173 in planktonic cells under aerobic growth conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33850153">Barraud21</a>].
<p>
Weight matrices for the DNA-binding site for ArcA-P have been obtained. The proposed binding site consists of 15 bp with a direct spaced repeat [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15728117">Favorov05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10216875">McGuire99</a>]. It has been suggested that multimerization, induced by phosphorylation, is a prerequisite for binding [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11527965">Jeon01</a>]. ArcA represses transcription by directly binding to the promoter or by binding to sites overlapping an activator-binding site [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16849788">Cho06a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15252051">Jeong04b</a>]. As an activator, it  appears to act as part of a nucleoprotein complex. For activation of <i>pfl</i>, a functional interaction between the ArcA and Fnr protein has been suggested [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1592804">Sawers92</a>]. For expression of <i>cydAB</i>, it has been shown that ArcA-P antagonizes H-NS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11123679">Govantes00</a>]. At the R1 P<sub>Y</sub> promoter, ArcA acts in conjunction with TraJ. ArcA represses and activates transcription solely by binding DNA, and it activates only indirectly when its binding interferes with the binding and repression of another transcriptional repressor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. The majority of ArcA-binding sites overlap the &sigma;<sup>70</sup> promoter recognition elements [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>].
<p>
ArcA is not an essential protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32108145">Miyake20</a>]. Under glucose-abundant conditions, the double mutant of <i>iclR arcA</i> causes an increase in biomass yield (47%) and reduction of acetate (70%) and CO<sub>2</sub> (16%) production. Under glucose-limited conditions, this double mutant exhibits an increase of biomass of only 13% [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21481254">Waegeman11</a>]. On the other hand, in an <i>arcA</i> mutant, the TCA cycle flux was increased 4.4 times above that of the wild type in the presence of nitrates, and the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio increased approximately 2-fold above that of the wild-type strain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22790675">Toya12</a>].
<p>
An exhaustive analysis of the ArcA response regulator was carried out, based on different experimental methodologies, High-throughputs (ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq), bioinformatic analysis, DNase I footprinting, and gene expression profiling, and the results showed that ArcA is a global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. ArcA-P directly regulates the expression of 85 operons under anaerobic growth conditions, where 74 operons are repressed and 11 are activated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. The proportion of phosphorylated ArcA is increased in aerobic conditions and the presence of carbon monoxide (CO) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26907100">Wareham16</a>]. It was shown that most ArcA-binding sites contain additional direct repeat (DR) elements as well as the two required for binding an ArcA dimer, and this finding provided a  novel insight into how ArcA accomplishes global regulation of gene expression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. More than 50% of the sites have additional DR elements, and the majority of ArcA-binding sites contain three to five DR elements, predominantly at a CTC spacing of 11 bp [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. The variations in the number, spacing, location, and predicted strength of DR elements within the chromosomal ArcA-binding regions suggest plasticity in the architecture of ArcA-binding sites for either repressed or activated operons [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>].
<p>
The growth [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>] and the net final biomass produced in an <i>arcA</i> single-deletion mutants  growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions were affected relative to responses of the wild-type strain (<i>Escherichia coli</i> strain BW25113) grown in the same conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>]. <i>arcA</i> deletion increased expression of genes involved in acetate assimilation and uptake and also genes involved in the TCA cycle [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29193870">Veeravalli18</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. The mutant also caused decreased nucleotide synthesis, decreased glucose and ammonia uptake rates, and enhanced nitrogen transport and accumulation of amino acids and their precursors, as well as derepression of alternate carbon metabolic proteins [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. The activities of some transcription factors appear to be enhanced (ArgR, NtrC, NrdR) in the arcA mutant, whereas others are diminished (PuuR) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>] et al. reported a relative increase in glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate in an arcA mutant. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield in the mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>].
<p>
ArcA promotes dehydration tolerance, both independently and through ArcZ or RpoS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29457688">Chen18c</a>].
<p>
The accumulation of the protein ArcA is decreased during iron-limiting conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31235512">Zupok19</a>]. A negative correlation between cellular growth and the copy number of the proteins ArcA has been reported [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35694815">Parisutham22</a>].
<p>
ArcA is a flux sensor for the oxygen consumption rate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32383263">Nochino20</a>].
<p>
Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of ArcA appears to increase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33731833">Deter21</a>].
<p>
Deletion of <i>arcA</i> and <i>gutM</i> under three different antibiotics, cefixime, ciprofloxacin, and chloramphenicol, significantly suppressed resistance evolution, which was not caused by epistatic interactions with mutations known to confer drug resistance [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32144279">Horinouchi20</a>].
<p>
When cells are grown in acetate as a carbon source, the knockout mutants of <i>arcA</i> and <i>fis</i> show an improved growth rate and enhanced acetate uptake [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35416487">Jindal22</a>]. This is a consequence of the reprogramming of the carbon metabolic flux generated by the mutants [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35416487">Jindal22</a>].
<p>
A review of the regulation of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis and molybdoenzyme gene expression via molybdenum and iron by FNR, NarXL/QP, Fur, and ArcA has been published [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31517366">Zupok19a</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35442087">Brown22</a>]</comment>

It acts primarily as a negative transcriptional regulator under anaerobic conditions. ArcA represses operons involved in respiratory metabolism, including those that encode products such as the tricarboxylic acid cycle enzymes, enzymes of the glyoxylate shunt, and enzymes of the pathway for fatty acid degradation [Iuchi91, Gunsalus94, Lin91]. In addition, ArcA acts as a repressor for rpoS transcription [Mika05]. ArcA also activates a few operons encoding proteins involved in fermentative metabolism [Brondsted94, Lynch96]. It has been identified as global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [Park13d]. Microarray analyses have identified a large number of genes affected by ArcA and have revealed that the Arc system and the FNR regulatory network overlap to a much greater extent than previously estimated [Salmon05, Liu04a, Perrenoud05, Iyer21]. It has been suggested that the most significant role of ArcA is under microaerobic conditions, while that of FNR is under more strictly anaerobic conditions [Alexeeva03, Levanon05]. For full expression of arcA both FNR and ArcA are required [Compan94]. Distinct functional roles for both regulators have been proposed, and it has been shown that there is little direct coregulation of the two [Park13d].

ArcA is a response regulator and is activated as a DNA-binding protein by phosphorylation [Jeon01]. The cognate sensor kinase ArcB is membrane associated and has three cytoplasmic domains; a transmitter, a receiver, and a phosphotransfer (HPt) domain [Ishige94, Iuchi92a]. Under anaerobic conditions ArcA is phosphorylated in a phosphorelay reaction that involves phosphotransfer from the autophosphorylated transmitter domain of ArcB to the receiver and Hpt domain of ArcB and finally to the receiver domain of ArcA [Kwon00c, Tsuzuki95, Georgellis97]. Autophosphorylation of ArcB is stimulated by effectors such as d-lactate, pyruvate, and acetate [Georgellis99, Georgellis99]. Under aerobic conditions, the autokinase activity of ArcB is inhibited by quinone electron carriers [Georgellis01, Malpica04], and unphosphorylated ArcB promotes the dephosphorylation of ArcA-P by a reverse phosphorelay reaction [Georgellis98, PenaSandoval05]. It has been suggested that ArcA may also be subject to cross-regulation by other, unknown sensor kinases [Mika05, Oshima02, Kato07a]. Z nucleotides [ZMP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-monophosphate) and/or ZTP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-triphosphate)] can act as direct phosphodonors to ArcA in vivo, activating it in an ArcB-independent manner [VazquezCiros20].

ArcA is a member of the OmpR/PhoB subfamily of response regulators and consists of an N-terminal receiver domain and a C-terminal helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain [Mizuno97]. The crystal structures of the receiver domain of ArcA in the presence and absence of the phosphoryl analog BeF3- have been solved [ToroRoman05a]. In the crystal structures, the receiver domain forms a symmetric dimer.

ArcA appears to be S-nitrosylated on Cys173 in planktonic cells under aerobic growth conditions [Barraud21].

Weight matrices for the DNA-binding site for ArcA-P have been obtained. The proposed binding site consists of 15 bp with a direct spaced repeat [Favorov05, McGuire99]. It has been suggested that multimerization, induced by phosphorylation, is a prerequisite for binding [Jeon01]. ArcA represses transcription by directly binding to the promoter or by binding to sites overlapping an activator-binding site [Cho06a, Jeong04b]. As an activator, it appears to act as part of a nucleoprotein complex. For activation of pfl, a functional interaction between the ArcA and Fnr protein has been suggested [Sawers92]. For expression of cydAB, it has been shown that ArcA-P antagonizes H-NS [Govantes00]. At the R1 PY promoter, ArcA acts in conjunction with TraJ. ArcA represses and activates transcription solely by binding DNA, and it activates only indirectly when its binding interferes with the binding and repression of another transcriptional repressor [Park13d]. The majority of ArcA-binding sites overlap the σ70 promoter recognition elements [Park13d].

ArcA is not an essential protein [Miyake20]. Under glucose-abundant conditions, the double mutant of iclR arcA causes an increase in biomass yield (47%) and reduction of acetate (70%) and CO2 (16%) production. Under glucose-limited conditions, this double mutant exhibits an increase of biomass of only 13% [Waegeman11]. On the other hand, in an arcA mutant, the TCA cycle flux was increased 4.4 times above that of the wild type in the presence of nitrates, and the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio increased approximately 2-fold above that of the wild-type strain [Toya12].

An exhaustive analysis of the ArcA response regulator was carried out, based on different experimental methodologies, High-throughputs (ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq), bioinformatic analysis, DNase I footprinting, and gene expression profiling, and the results showed that ArcA is a global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [Park13d]. ArcA-P directly regulates the expression of 85 operons under anaerobic growth conditions, where 74 operons are repressed and 11 are activated [Park13d]. The proportion of phosphorylated ArcA is increased in aerobic conditions and the presence of carbon monoxide (CO) [Wareham16]. It was shown that most ArcA-binding sites contain additional direct repeat (DR) elements as well as the two required for binding an ArcA dimer, and this finding provided a novel insight into how ArcA accomplishes global regulation of gene expression [Park13d]. More than 50% of the sites have additional DR elements, and the majority of ArcA-binding sites contain three to five DR elements, predominantly at a CTC spacing of 11 bp [Park13d]. The variations in the number, spacing, location, and predicted strength of DR elements within the chromosomal ArcA-binding regions suggest plasticity in the architecture of ArcA-binding sites for either repressed or activated operons [Park13d].

The growth [Iyer21, Kargeti17] and the net final biomass produced in an arcA single-deletion mutants growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions were affected relative to responses of the wild-type strain (Escherichia coli strain BW25113) grown in the same conditions [Kargeti17]. arcA deletion increased expression of genes involved in acetate assimilation and uptake and also genes involved in the TCA cycle [Veeravalli18, Iyer21]. The mutant also caused decreased nucleotide synthesis, decreased glucose and ammonia uptake rates, and enhanced nitrogen transport and accumulation of amino acids and their precursors, as well as derepression of alternate carbon metabolic proteins [Iyer21]. The activities of some transcription factors appear to be enhanced (ArgR, NtrC, NrdR) in the arcA mutant, whereas others are diminished (PuuR) [Iyer21]. [Kargeti18] et al. reported a relative increase in glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate in an arcA mutant. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield in the mutant [Kargeti18].

ArcA promotes dehydration tolerance, both independently and through ArcZ or RpoS [Chen18c].

The accumulation of the protein ArcA is decreased during iron-limiting conditions [Zupok19]. A negative correlation between cellular growth and the copy number of the proteins ArcA has been reported [Parisutham22].

ArcA is a flux sensor for the oxygen consumption rate [Nochino20].

Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of ArcA appears to increase [Deter21].

Deletion of arcA and gutM under three different antibiotics, cefixime, ciprofloxacin, and chloramphenicol, significantly suppressed resistance evolution, which was not caused by epistatic interactions with mutations known to confer drug resistance [Horinouchi20].

When cells are grown in acetate as a carbon source, the knockout mutants of arcA and fis show an improved growth rate and enhanced acetate uptake [Jindal22]. This is a consequence of the reprogramming of the carbon metabolic flux generated by the mutants [Jindal22].

A review of the regulation of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis and molybdoenzyme gene expression via molybdenum and iron by FNR, NarXL/QP, Fur, and ArcA has been published [Zupok19a].

observed.xml: To test if l-lyxose itself or an intermediate metabolite was the inducer of the arabinose system, a Tn5 insertion mutant in the rhaA gene (encoding rhamnose isomerase) was obtained from strain JA134 (strain JA199) by using phage λ 467 (b221 cIts857 rex::Tn5 Oam29 Pam80) (4). This mutant was selected by its inability to utilize l-lyxose and the inability to excrete l-rhamnulose when grown in the presence of l-rhamnose. The precise location of the insertion in rhaA was assessed by cloning and sequencing the chromosomal region close to the Tn5 by using an internal sequence of the transposon as a primer. Induction of the ara operon by l-lyxose in strain JA199 indicated that this compound was directly activating the arabinose operon expression.

observed.xml: Expression plasmid pPlaR used for over-expression and purification of His-tagged PlaR was constructed essentially according to the standard procedure9. For construction of plasmid for PlaR expression, a DNA fragment corresponding to the PlaR-coding sequence was amplified by PCR and cloned into pET21a(+) (Novagen) between NdeI and NotI sites, leading to construct pPlaR. For protein expression, pPlaR plasmid was transformed into E. coli BL21 (DE3). Transformants were grown in LB medium and PlaR expression was induced by adding 1 mM IPTG in the middle of exponential growth phase. PlaR protein was purified by the affinity purification procedure with use of a Ni-nitrilotriacetic acid (NTA) agarose column. The affinity-purified PlaR protein was stored frozen in the storage buffer at −80 °C until use. Protein purity was more than 95% as checked by SDS-PAGE.

locator: XPath /article/body/sec[4]/sec[4]/p; paragraph containing 'The gel shift assay was performed'
assertion: Gel shifts used BW25113-derived promoter probes and buffer containing Tris pH 7.8, NaCl and magnesium acetate. These conditions support chosen solution species without measuring ligand protonation or anomer purity.

observed.xml: The gel shift assay was performed as described previously54. The probes of promoter region were synthesized using a set of primers (Table S1a), BW25113 genome as a template, and Ex Taq DNA polymerase (TAKARA). For gel shift assays, 0.5 pmol each of the probes was incubated at 37 °C for 20 min with various amounts of PlaR in 15 ml of gel shift buffer consisting of 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.8 at 4 °C, 150 mM NaCl, and 3 mM Mg acetate. In the case of addition of chemical compounds, 1 ml of various concentrations of chemical compounds was added and incubated for another 20 min. After addition of a DNA dye solution, the mixture was directly subjected to 5% PAGE. The probe DNA in gels was stained by Gel-Red (Biotium) and detected using LAS-4000 IR multi-colour (GE healthcare).

locator: XPath /article/body/sec[2]/sec[7]/p[2]; paragraph containing 'We then examined the possible influence'
assertion: L-ascorbate increased the yiaK reporter in wild-type BW25113, with little additional activation in the plaR mutant. Conditions were 0.2% alpha-D-galacturonate or 30 mM L-ascorbate; this is operon-expression context, not complete L-lyxose flux.

observed.xml: We then examined the possible influence of the two effective metabolites, L-ascorbate and α-D-galacturonate, on the induction of the yiaK operon. Both the metabolites induced a dose-dependent dissociation in vitro of PlaR from the PlaR-yiaK promoter complex (Fig. 8b). This finding indicates that both L-ascorbate and α-D-galacturonate play a regulatory role in controlling the activity of the PlaR repressor. To confirm the activation in vivo of PlaR by these two compounds, we carried out a yiaK reporter assay in wild-type and a plaR-deletion mutant. To identify the specificity of the effector ligand of PlaR inactivation, we measured the activity of the yiaK promoter in the presence of 0.2% of α-D-galacturonate or 30 mM of L-ascorbate (Fig. 6). In wild-type strain, the yiaK promoter was activated in the presence of α-D-galacturonate or L-ascorbate (Fig. 6a). In contrast, in plaR knock-out mutant, little activation of the yiaK promoter was observed (Fig. 6b). The effect of L-ascorbate found in this study is in good agreement with the reported modest activation of the yiaK promoter by L-ascorbate10. We then conclude that PlaR recognizes α-D-galacturonate and L-ascorbate as its effectors.

observed.xml:
PlaR was shown to repress some of the operons or genes for utilization of plant-derived nutrients. In order to identify a possible inducer ligand(s) for derepression of the yiaK operon (the major regulatory target of PlaR), we first tried to identify metabolites affecting the binding in vitro of PlaR to the yiaK promoter. First we tested 10 mM concentrations of various carbon sources, and found significant reduction of PlaR binding for two metabolites, L-ascorbate and α-D-galacturonate (Fig. 8a). However, D-glucuronate, another degradation product of pectin, did not affect PlaR binding to the yiaK promoter.

assertion: Glucose enhanced the divergent yiaJ/plaR reporter while repressing yiaK-S. This is coordinated carbon-source-dependent expression in the examined reporter backgrounds, not direct glucose binding to PlaR.

observed.xml: Cultures of strain JA134 carrying φ(yiaK-lacZ) grown in the presence of glucose, both aerobically and anaerobically, showed lower β-galactosidase activities, indicating that glucose produced catabolite repression in this promoter. The addition of cyclic AMP (cAMP) to a 5 mM concentration partially recovered the activity in the presence of glucose. The threefold increased expression of φ(yiaK-lacZ) by growth on succinate (Table 2), which is considered a poor carbon source, also confirmed the regulation of this operon by carbon sources. In contrast, the presence of glucose enhanced the promoter function of the regulator, as indicated by the increased β-galactosidase activity of φ(yiaJ-lacZ). No relevant effect of the cAMP addition was observed in this case. This is further supported by the increase in the expression of (yiaJ-lacZ) fusion (510 Miller units) and the reduction of the expression of (yiaK-lacZ) fusion (55 Miller units) in strain JA186 lacking Crp. Thus, yiaK-S transcription is coordinately repressed in the presence of glucose by both the effect of the absence of cAMP-Crp binding to the promoter and the increase in repressor synthesis.

L-fucose modestly increased the yiaK-S reporter in ECL1 under the 2000 screening conditions, while JA134 was constitutively high. The physiological inducer was then unresolved; direct PlaR ligand binding was not shown.

observed.xml: Among 80 different compounds tested, only l-fucose and l-ascorbate resulted in modestly increased expression of β-galactosidase activity (Table 2). No induction was seen with any of the other compounds, including pentoses, hexoses, other derivative sugars, mono- and dicarboxylate organic acids, and related compounds listed in Materials and Methods. The possibility of the presence of the inducer in animal gut or lung mucus was explored by using rat specimens suspended in minimal medium and autoclaved. These solutions were added to CAA medium at a final concentration of 0.1%. No induction of β-galactosidase activity was detected by growth in any of these cultures.
